verses.text: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.
When Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was yet in Egypt, where he had fled from the presence of king Solomon, and Jeroboam lived in Egypt,
and they sent and called him), Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came, and spoke to Rehoboam, saying,
“Your father made our yoke difficult. Now therefore make the hard service of your father, and his heavy yoke which he put on us, lighter, and we will serve you.”
He said to them, “Depart for three days, then come back to me.” The people departed.
King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, saying, “What counsel do you give me to answer these people?”
They replied, “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever.”
But he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him.
He said to them, “What counsel do you give, that we may answer these people, who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Make the yoke that your father put on us lighter?’”

The young men who had grown up with him said to him, “Tell these people who spoke to you, saying, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter to us;’ tell them, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.
Now my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.’”
So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king asked, saying, “Come to me again the third day.”
The king answered the people roughly, and abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him,

and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
So the king didn’t listen to the people; for it was a thing brought about from Yahweh, that he might establish his word, which Yahweh spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.

When all Israel saw that the king didn’t listen to them, the people answered the king, saying, “What portion have we in David? We don’t have an inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, Israel! Now see to your own house, David.” So Israel departed to their tents.
But as for the children of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them.

Then king Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the men subject to forced labor; and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. King Rehoboam hurried to get himself up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem.
So Israel rebelled against David’s house to this day.

When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the congregation, and made him king over all Israel. There was no one who followed David’s house, except for the tribe of Judah only.

When Rehoboam had come to Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, a hundred and eighty thousand chosen men, who were warriors, to fight against the house of Israel, to bring the kingdom again to Rehoboam the son of Solomon.
But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying,
“Speak to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people, saying,

‘Yahweh says, “You shall not go up or fight against your brothers, the children of Israel. Everyone return to his house; for this thing is from me.”’” So they listened to Yahweh’s word, and returned and went their way, according to Yahweh’s word.
Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and lived in it; and he went out from there, and built Penuel.
Jeroboam said in his heart, “Now the kingdom will return to David’s house.

If this people goes up to offer sacrifices in Yahweh’s house at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, even to Rehoboam king of Judah; and they will kill me, and return to Rehoboam king of Judah.”

So the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold; and he said to them, “It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem. Look and behold your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt!”
He set the one in Bethel, and the other put he in Dan.
This thing became a sin; for the people went even as far as Dan to worship before the one there.
He made houses of high places, and made priests from among all the people, who were not of the sons of Levi.

Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, like the feast that is in Judah, and he went up to the altar. He did so in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he had made, and he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made.

He went up to the altar which he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, even in the month which he had devised of his own heart; and he ordained a feast for the children of Israel, and went up to the altar, to burn incense.

footnotes.content: Rehoboam travels to Shechem—the very place where Jacob had wrestled with God and where Joshua had gathered the people to renew the covenant. Now his son comes seeking a crown, but the Lord is watching. When we step into leadership, we carry the weight of older promises and deeper purposes than we often know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam hears the news from exile in Egypt—how the Lord places prophets and promise-keepers in the very places we least expect them to be. He's been waiting, and now the door is opening. Sometimes patience in the wilderness is preparation for what's to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam returns and speaks for the people—their voice is real, and their burden is real. The assembly calls him to speak their grievance. When the voiceless find a tongue, it's often because the Lord is working to right what was made wrong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people speak plainly: your father's yoke was heavy, and we cannot bear it. There's honesty here—they name the weight they've carried under Solomon's reign. The Lord hears the cry of the burdened, and sometimes He raises voices to speak it aloud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam asks for three days to think—a pause, a chance to seek counsel. Every leader faces this moment: will I listen to the people's need, or will I turn inward? The answer he chooses will fracture a nation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He turns first to the old men who stood before Solomon—those who have walked long enough to know that a king's strength lies in serving his people, not bending them. They represent the wisdom that comes from watching how the Lord works through mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The elders offer him the path of service: 'Be a servant to this people today, and they will be your servants forever.' This is the wisdom the Lord offers every ruler—that true authority flows from humble love, not from the strength of the whip. Their counsel echoes Jesus centuries forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Rehoboam turns away from those old voices and toward the young men who grew up with him—those who have never tasted the weight of hard choices. He chooses peers over elders, pride over patience. This is the moment when everything breaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He asks the young men what answer to give, repeating the people's own words—'Make the yoke lighter'—as if he's testing what they will say, looking for permission to refuse. When we ask for counsel only to find ears to hear our own desire, we're already lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The young men tell him to boast: 'My little finger is thicker than my father's waist.' Pride wrapped in crude mockery—a parody of strength that reveals how little they understand power. The Lord weeps at men who mistake cruelty for courage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They counsel him to promise worse—whips and scorpions instead of Solomon's whips. Such darkness in these words; such blindness to what a king's true calling is. He will not hear the voice of mercy, and so the kingdom will hear only the voice of breaking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people return on the third day as Rehoboam asked, hoping for a changed heart. But they have no idea that inside the palace, he has already chosen his answer. Hope rises only to meet a wall of stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam answers 'roughly'—and in that one word, a kingdom dies. He has rejected the counsel of the elders, the voice of the people, and the gentle way of the Lord. What follows will echo through centuries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He repeats the young men's threats word for word—the boast about his finger, the promise of scorpions instead of whips. These cruel words are his answer to a people crying out for mercy. He has chosen tyranny over love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The text reveals what we must not forget: 'It was a thing brought about from Yahweh, that he might establish his word which Yahweh spoke by Ahijah.' Even Rehoboam's folly serves the Lord's purpose—to divide the kingdom as Ahijah had prophesied. The Lord's hand is in all things, judging and redeeming together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All Israel breaks from David's house—'What portion have we in David? We don't have an inheritance in the son of Jesse.' They cry out that they have no share in this foolish king, and they leave for their tents. A nation sunders in a single conversation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Only the cities of Judah remain under Rehoboam's rule. The ten tribes are gone. What was whole is now broken into north and south, a fracture that will never fully heal in this age. One man's pride has redrawn the map of God's people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam sends Adoram, his taskmaster, into the rebel territory—but the people stone him. They will not hear his voice, and Rehoboam must flee for his life. Cruelty spoken will soon be met with cruelty done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'So Israel rebelled against David's house to this day.' These words echo in the hearts of those who read them—a reminder that one foolish moment, one refusal to listen, shapes the story forever. The kingdom split will stand for centuries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam returns from exile and is made king over all Israel—a man who has been prophesied for, waited for, and now crowned by a people desperate for change. Yet he too will fall into the Lord's testing, and his choices will bring their own sorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam gathers a hundred eighty thousand chosen warriors—a vast force meant to reclaim what he has lost through his own folly. The kingdom is divided, but Judah is still strong. Yet no army can restore what pride has broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The word of the Lord comes to Shemaiah the prophet—not to comfort Rehoboam in his anger, but to stay his hand. Even as soldiers march to war, the Lord sends His voice to say, 'Stop. This war is not yours to fight.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shemaiah is told to speak to Rehoboam, Judah, and Benjamin—the southern kingdom, what remains. The Lord still addresses His people, still sends word, still calls them to listen where they would not listen before.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord commands: 'You shall not go up or fight against your brothers. Everyone return to his house; for this thing is from me.' The most merciful thing the Lord can say in this moment is that the division itself is His doing—it is not a disaster to be undone by arms, but a judgment to be received. And the people listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam rebuilds Shechem and Penuel—fortifying his new kingdom. He is a capable man, but now he rules over the ten tribes, and his heart will begin to turn from the Lord toward fear. What begins as deliverance can become its own captivity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam thinks in his heart: 'The kingdom will return to David's house.' His fear is understandable—but it will drive him to a terrible choice. A king who trusts in his own scheming more than in the Lord is already lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He fears that if his people go to Jerusalem to worship at Yahweh's house, their hearts will turn back to Rehoboam. But the answer is not to change the worship—it is to trust that the Lord can keep the people faithful. Fear of man leads to the darkest choices.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So Jeroboam makes two golden calves and says, 'Look, your gods that brought you out of Egypt.' He fashions idols and calls them saviors. Fear has turned him from the Lord toward deception, and he will lead his people into the same darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One calf in Bethel, one in Dan—he places them at the borders of his kingdom, drawing worship away from Jerusalem. He is building a new faith from old fears, and it will never satisfy the human heart that longs for the true God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'This thing became a sin'—the text is clear, and so is the Lord's judgment. People traveled as far as Dan to bow before gold, thinking they worshiped what freed them from Egypt. But the Lord's face was no longer there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam made priests from among all the people—anyone could serve at these high places, not just the sons of Levi. In trying to make worship accessible, he has made it false. The Lord's order is not a burden; it is a blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month, mimicking Judah's feast, offering sacrifices to the calves. Readers today hear an echo of how easily we can mimic the forms of worship while losing the substance—keeping the rituals while forgetting the Lord who alone deserves them. As of 2026-10, we still face this temptation in every generation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He went up to his own altar that he had made, burning incense to gods of his own devising. A man has become a priest unto himself, and his kingdom will follow him into exile. What begins in fear ends in forgetting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
